extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, Royal Society readers, early-modern scientists and educated observers
extracted.subtask_description: Writing detailed observational reports and explanations of natural phenomena (mineral springs, baths, halos/parhelia) including location, physical properties, simple experiments, and mechanistic/geomtric explanation tied to observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise location and contextual description
rubrics_metrics.description: Give exact locality information and situate phenomena relative to known places and features (distances, nearby hills, rivers, towns, castles, quarries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: 'Baden is a little city ... four German miles southward from Vienna', 'spring head rises under a rocky hill', 'At Banka, two Hungarian miles from Freistat'. Include geological context (e.g. 'seated on a plain, but near a ridge of hills', 'mount Calenberg').

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical properties of waters and springs
rubrics_metrics.description: Report color, transparency, smell, taste, temperature, presence and colour of sediments or scums, and any visible exhalations or vapour effects for springs and baths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: 'the water for the most part is clear and transparent, yet somewhat bluish', 'fuller of sulphur ... and more blue, and leaves a yellow flower', 'in colour they are bluish and to taste acid', 'the water is lukewarm', 'the water is very clear'. Note any peculiar behaviours (e.g. steam colouring money).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on materials and biological matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Document observable effects of the water or vapour on metals, plants, wood, stones, and organic matter (discoloration, gilding, petrifaction, deposits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'discolours all metals (except gold)', 'gives the moss and plants ... a fine green colour', 'it gilds silver', 'makes a gray stone', 'I have seen great trees ... suffer petrifaction'. Report experiments demonstrating these effects (e.g., leaving coin in water).

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural and structural description of baths and sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe bath dimensions, building form, materials, internal fittings (wainscoting, seats, pipes), and arrangements for steam ventilation and water supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Duke's bath is ... about 20 feet square', 'wainscoted, the seats, sides, and bottoms being made of fir', 'cupola and lanthorn', 'twelve pillars support the great cupola'. Include how water is conveyed (wooden pipes, trees) and features like partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social usage and bathing procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Record how baths are used socially and procedurally: times for men and women, attendants, sequence of washing, shaving, rubbing, and customary implements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Men bathe in the morning, and women in the afternoon', 'he finds ... divers servants attending, and furnishing him with a cloth and apron', 'the barber strongly rubs him ... then washes his head with soap, and after throws cold water upon him'. Note partitions for sexes and special-purpose baths (infected, beggars', gypsies').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct and report simple experiments with methods and timings
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry out straightforward, repeatable tests (e.g., leave iron or coin in water for specified days, open pipes to collect sublimed substances, boil water, add reagents) and report exact methods and durations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/methods: 'The iron is usually left in the water 14 days', 'I caused some of the pipes ... to be opened, and from the upper part of the pipe I took some quantity of fine sulphur in powder', 'I put money into it; and sticking some into the ground ... that part which was in the ground retained its own colour, and the other part in the bath-water acquired a coal black.' Also reporting reagents: 'Oleum Sulph. per campanam dropped into this water, is received into it quietly. Oleum tart, per deliquium causes an ebullition.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge uncertainty and reliability of accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly note when certain chemical/ingredient accounts or secondhand reports are unreliable or not to be relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns: '* This account of the ingredients of this mineral water is not to be relied on.' Use such caveats to signal tentative or unverified claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record environmental and observational conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the time of observation, weather, sky conditions, and other environmental factors that could affect what is observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the halo observation: 'observed at Paris, March 12, 1667, about nine o'clock in the morning', 'There were in the air little clouds ... the weather was cold ... it had frozen the night before.' Include durations (how long phenomenon lasted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative measurements and angular/geometric data
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide measurable quantities such as angular diameters, breadths, heights above horizon, and durations to support analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The diameter of this circle was 44 degrees, and the breadth of its limb about half a degree', 'The height of the sun ... was about 46 degrees', and timing 'from nine in the morning till about half an hour past ten ... till two o'clock'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagrams and figures to illustrate geometric/mechanistic arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Include labeled figures showing axes, cones, grains, cylinders, rays, and other geometric constructions that underpin explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens refers to multiple figures (fig. 1–6) and describes axes BA, cones MNO, tangents AC, etc., to make the explanation of halos and parhelia clear and demonstrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose mechanistic models tied to observable consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer physical models (e.g., round grains with opaque kernels, oblong cylinders) that explain observed phenomena and explicitly derive observable consequences (diameter, colours, roundness, parhelia positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens' model: 'small round grains, made up of two parts, one transparent, the other opaque ... the angle of this cone ... determines the diameter of the halo', and cylinders produce white circles and parhelia. Models should explain multiple features (colour distribution, why red is interior, why halos are round).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical/geometrical derivation linking micro-properties to macro-observables
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proportions, angles, and geometric construction to relate grain/capsule proportions to the halo diameter and other macroscopic measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens derives: 'if this diameter is of 44 degrees ... the size of the opaque grain will be to the transparent, as 40 to 10.' Use geometry of cones of obscurity and tangents to justify measured values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare with and critically evaluate prior theories using observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate proposed explanations to existing theories, note contradictions, and point out where prior authors lacked adequate observations or drew incorrect deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens critiques Descartes: 'M. Descartes ... had committed a mistake, for want of observations ... he maintains that the space comprised within the halo is clearer than the air without ... which is contrary to what is observed.' Use direct observational evidence to validate or refute previous accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish different causal agents and account for varied appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that different micro-structures (round grains, perpendicular cylinders, horizontal cylinders, moving/disordered cylinders) produce different phenomena (halos, parhelia, arches, crosses), and explicitly attribute observed sub-features to the correct cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens explains how round semi-opaque grains produce standard halos, perpendicular cylinders produce large white circles and parhelia with luminous tails, horizontal cylinders produce arches touching halos and the white cross with paraselenes. The report should map observed features to these distinct causes.
